Urdu وقعت (waqa'at/waqat = value, worth, esteem) gives "be-waqat" = "of no value/insignificant" (describing the lowly fluid). Roman substitutes "waqar" (dignity/gravitas), a different Urdu word (وقار) with a different, though similar-sounding, meaning ("without dignity" vs "of no worth"). Likely a transliteration mix-up between two similar-sounding but distinct words.

Urdu says "باحکمت" (full of/possessing wisdom); Roman substitutes "Hakeem" (wise), a different word that echoes the Arabic ayah rather than transliterating Junagarhi's actual Urdu word choice. Same general sense, different word.

Stray extra "h": "chakhho" instead of the corpus's standard "chakho" (taste, imperative) used elsewhere for the same Urdu word چکھو (e.g. 32:14, twice, "maza chakho"). Simple doubling typo, not a different word.
Stray doubled vowel: "dozakhii" instead of the standard "dozakhi" (of/belonging to hell) used elsewhere in the corpus for دوزخی. Not a different word, just an extra "i".

Urdu دیں here is the past-tense verb "gave" (feminine plural object daleelein), pronounced deen -- "We gave them the religion's clear proofs." Roman "din" reads as a different word, "day" (din), not the verb. Same verse elsewhere correctly uses deen-forms (deen ki), so this is an isolated vowel slip, not a style choice.

اعلان (announcement/openly) is spelled "ailaan" elsewhere in the corpus (9:1 "bezaari ka ailaan"). Here the same root is romanised "aalaan", a different-sounding, non-standard form. Likely a vowel slip rather than a deliberate spelling choice, though this exact phrase علی الاعلان has no other occurrence to confirm against.

مڈبھیڑ (encounter/clash) has a retroflex ڈ (d-sound), giving "mudbher". Roman "muthbher" swaps in a "th" sound (as in ٹھ), which is a different consonant and reads as a garbled/unfamiliar word. No other occurrence of this word in the corpus to cross-check against.

Source has مدددگار with an extra د (three د's), a typo for مددگار "helper." Roman already silently reads it correctly as "madadgaar" -- no Roman change needed, but per plan §1.2 C this should be logged in data/roman-urdu/source-errata.tsv.

Urdu places بزرگ وبلند as apposition describing "پروردگار" ("Lord, Great and Exalted"), with no izafat marker between the two. Roman inserts "-e-" after Parwardigaar, turning it into a genitive ("the Greatness-and-Exaltedness of the Lord") rather than the appositive description Junagarhi wrote. "Buzurg-o-Buland" (and-compound) itself is fine.

Urdu پھیرتا (pherta, from پھیرنا "to turn away/avert" -- transitive) is rendered "phirta," which reads as پھرتا (phirna, "to wander/roam" -- intransitive), a different verb. The idiom "munh pherna" (to turn one's face away) is the intended sense here and is correctly spelled "pher" elsewhere in the corpus (e.g. surah 92:16 "munh pher liya").
